# Row and Completeness Validations {#sec-row-validations}

```{python}
#| include: false
import pointblank as pb
pb.config(report_incl_header=False, report_incl_footer=False)
```

Column checks ask whether a value is acceptable. Row checks ask whether a whole row is acceptable,
and some problems only show up when you look at rows. A row can have a valid value in every column
and still be wrong, either because it duplicates another row or because a field it needs is empty.
To catch those problems, the row has to be the unit of validation rather than the individual cell.

This chapter covers the two row-level checks that come up most often: distinctness and
completeness. Most of the chapter is about the decisions each one involves. For distinctness, that
means choosing which columns make up the key. For completeness, it means deciding which fields are
required and which are optional. Both checks produce one test unit per row, so their reports read
like the per-row column checks of @sec-column-validations and tell you how many rows are affected.
Some other row-level checks, like rules that tie several columns together or judgments made by an
AI model, have their own chapters, and we point to those at the end.

We use `game_revenue` for realistic scale and the smaller `small_table` when a short result makes
the behavior easier to see.

```{python}
game_revenue = pb.load_dataset(dataset="game_revenue", tbl_type="polars")
small_table = pb.load_dataset(dataset="small_table", tbl_type="polars")
```

## Row distinctness

Duplicate rows cause trouble that is easy to miss. They inflate counts and averages, and they can
make later steps process the same record twice. They also usually point to a problem earlier in the
pipeline, such as a deduplication step that failed or a join that matched more rows than expected.
The `rows_distinct()` method finds duplicates, and most of the work in using it is deciding what
"duplicate" should mean.

### Checking whole-row uniqueness

With no arguments, `rows_distinct()` compares entire rows and checks that no two are identical
across every column. The `small_table` dataset has one exact duplicate, which the check finds.

```{python}
(
    pb.Validate(data=small_table)
    .rows_distinct()
    .interrogate()
)
```
